intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and a clerk at the registrar's office.

turns.text: Hi, I ordered an official transcript about ten days ago for a summer research program, but they just emailed me saying it never arrived.
Let me check your order. Okay, it shows the transcript was printed and mailed on the fourth.
Mailed? I thought it would go electronically. Their deadline is Friday.
Well, on the order form, you chose paper delivery. That's probably why it's taking so long. Does the program accept electronic transcripts?
Yes, actually. That's what they prefer.
Then the simplest thing is to place a new order and choose the electronic option. It usually arrives within a few hours. There's a small fee, but I can waive it, since the first one never got there.
That'd be great. Can I do it here?
Sure. Use the computer by the window, and I'll approve it as soon as you submit.

questions.prompt: What is the student's problem?
options: His summer program has moved its application deadline
He was charged twice for a single transcript order
A transcript he ordered has not reached a program
His transcript lists a course that he never took
questions.explanation: He explains that the research program says his transcript never arrived.

questions.prompt: Why has the transcript been delayed?
options: He selected paper delivery on the order form.
The office printed it with the wrong address.
The program refuses to accept mailed documents.
His account had an unpaid fee on it.
questions.explanation: The clerk points out that he chose paper delivery, which is why it is taking so long.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and a clerk at the campus parking office.

turns.text: Hi, I found a warning on my windshield this morning, but I have a student parking permit. It's hanging right on the mirror.
Let me see. Okay, the permit's valid, but the license plate on our record doesn't match the car that was parked in Lot C.
Oh. I sold my old car last month and got a new one. I didn't know I had to tell anyone.
Yeah, the permit's tied to your plate number, not just the tag. Our cameras scan plates, so the system thought your car didn't have a permit.
So do I need to buy a new permit?
No, you can just update the plate in your parking account online. It takes a couple of minutes. And since this was only a warning, there's no fine.
Great. I'll do it as soon as I get home.
Do it before tomorrow morning, though. The next one would be an actual ticket.

questions.prompt: Why does the student go to the parking office?
options: To buy a new permit for a car she just purchased
To ask why she got a warning despite her permit
To report that her permit tag was stolen
To appeal a fine she received in Lot C
questions.explanation: She says she found a warning on her car even though she has a valid permit.

questions.prompt: Why does the man tell the student to update her account before tomorrow?
options: The online system will be closed tomorrow.
Her current permit expires the next morning.
She could receive a real ticket next time.
The cameras in Lot C are being replaced.
questions.explanation: He says that the next violation would be an actual ticket, not a warning.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and an employee at the campus mailroom.

turns.text: Hi, I got a text saying my package was delivered to locker twelve, but the code doesn't open it. I've tried three times.
Let me look up your name. Kenji Watanabe? Okay, I see what happened. The package turned out to be too big for the lockers, so we kept it back here.
But the text gave me a locker number.
Yeah, the system sends that automatically, before we actually sort things. It's confusing, I know. We've asked for it to be fixed.
So can I just take it now?
Sure, I just need to see your student ID. It's a pretty big box, though. Did you walk here?
I did. Is it heavy?
Kind of. We have a cart you can borrow, as long as you bring it back by five.

questions.prompt: What is the conversation mainly about?
options: Reporting a locker that was damaged by a box
Changing the phone number used for delivery texts
Mailing a heavy package to an off-campus address
Picking up a package that was not in its locker
questions.explanation: The student's package was too big for the locker, so it was kept behind the counter.

questions.prompt: What does the woman offer the student?
options: A new code for locker twelve
Delivery of the box to his dorm
A larger locker for future packages
A cart for carrying his package
questions.explanation: She says he can borrow a cart if he returns it by five.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and an advisor at the international student office.

turns.text: Hi, Mr. Hendricks. I got an internship offer from an engineering firm downtown, and they want me to start June first. I just need you to sign something, right?
Congratulations! It's a bit more than a signature, though. Off-campus work needs authorization. The paperwork goes through our office, and then there's an outside review.
How long does that usually take?
Honestly, it varies. I've seen it come back in three weeks, and I've seen it take two months. And you can't start until it's approved. Not even unpaid training.
Two months? That would push me into August. Hmm. They did mention that some interns start in July.
Then that's a conversation worth having with them now, rather than in May. Employers tend to be flexible when they hear about it early.
Okay. I'll email the recruiter this afternoon. And I'll bring you the offer letter tomorrow.

questions.prompt: What is the conversation mainly about?
options: Whether unpaid training counts as work experience
What must happen before the student can begin a job
How the student can find a firm that hires summer interns
Why the firm decided to withdraw its offer
questions.explanation: The advisor explains that her internship requires authorization and a review that may take weeks.

questions.prompt: What will the student probably ask the recruiter?
options: Whether the firm could handle all of her paperwork
Whether her training could be unpaid
Whether she could work remotely in June
Whether she could begin later in the summer
questions.explanation: She mentions that some interns start in July, and the advisor encourages her to raise the timing with the employer early.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and a coordinator at the disability services office.

turns.text: Hi. Um, I'm not sure I'm in the right place. I broke my wrist skiing last weekend, and I've got two midterms coming up. I can't really write.
You're in the right place. A lot of students assume we only work with long-term conditions, but temporary injuries count too.
Oh. I was just going to email my professors and ask if I could type my answers.

You could, but each professor might handle it differently. If you register with us, even temporarily, we send one letter to all of them, and the arrangements are guaranteed. Extra time, a laptop, or someone to write for you.
That does sound easier. What do I need?
A note from the doctor who treated you, saying how long you'll be in the cast.
I've got a follow-up appointment on Thursday. I'll ask for one then.

questions.prompt: Why does the student go to the office?
options: To return a laptop he borrowed for exams
To schedule a follow-up visit with the doctor who treated him
To learn how to get help with exams after an injury
To find out whether he may skip his midterms
questions.explanation: He explains that his broken wrist will make it hard to write during his upcoming midterms.

questions.prompt: Why does the student say he is not sure he is in the right place?
options: He expected to meet his professors there instead.
He had been told to visit the health clinic first.
He assumed his injury was too brief to qualify.
He was unsure whether he had an appointment.
questions.explanation: The coordinator responds that many students wrongly assume only long-term conditions count, which shows his doubt was about his temporary injury.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and a staff member at the campus art museum.

turns.text: Hi, I'm looking for a painting called Harbor at Dusk. My art history assignment is to describe it in person, but it's not in the gallery the map shows.
Ah, yes. That one was taken down last week. It's being cleaned in our conservation lab.
Oh no. My paper's due in ten days. When will it be back?
Not until next month, unfortunately. But here's something you might like. The lab has a big glass window, and on Saturday mornings it's open to visitors. You can watch the conservators working on it.
So I could still see the actual painting?
Exactly. And honestly, you'd notice details nobody sees when it's hanging on the wall. You might want to check with your professor that it counts, though.
I will. Thanks so much.

questions.prompt: What is the student's problem?
options: Her museum map shows the wrong gallery hours
A painting she must study is not on display
Her professor rejected the painting she chose
A painting she wrote about has been damaged
questions.explanation: The painting she needs to describe was removed from the gallery to be cleaned.

questions.prompt: What does the man suggest?
options: Writing about a different painting instead
Viewing the painting through a lab window
Asking her professor for a ten-day extension
Using photos of the painting from the website
questions.explanation: He says that on Saturday mornings visitors can watch the conservators through the lab's glass window.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and an assistant at the language lab.

turns.text: Hi. I recorded my Spanish speaking assignment here yesterday, but my professor says the file she got was empty.
Hmm. Which booth were you in, and where did you save it?
Booth six, I think. I just saved it to the desktop and then uploaded it from there.
Ah, that might be it. If you upload while the recording program is still open, sometimes the file isn't finished saving yet. So it sends a blank copy.
And the original's still on the desktop?
Unfortunately, no. These computers erase everything overnight. You'll have to record it again.
Ugh. Okay. Is there a booth free now?
Booth two is open. Just close the program before you upload this time, and play the file back once to be sure.

questions.prompt: Why does the student come to the language lab?
options: The recording he submitted turned out to be blank.
His professor asked him to re-record in a quieter booth.
He cannot find the recording program.
He wants to reserve a booth for tomorrow.
questions.explanation: He says his professor received an empty file from him.

questions.prompt: Why is the original recording no longer available?
options: Another student recorded over it in booth six.
Lab computers delete files every night.
The professor's system removed it after upload.
It was saved in the wrong language folder.
questions.explanation: The assistant explains that the lab computers erase everything overnight.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and an attendant at the art studio supply room.

turns.text: Hi, I need four more bags of the red clay. I'm building a big piece for my final project.
I can only give you one this week. Our delivery got delayed, so it's one bag per student until it comes.
One? That'll barely cover the base.
Have you looked at the reclaim bins? That's all the scraps people throw back, mixed with water and dried out again. It's free, and you can take as much as you want.
I thought that stuff was kind of lumpy. I don't want my piece cracking in the kiln.
It can be, if you don't wedge it well. But half the seniors use nothing else. If you mix it with your fresh bag, you'll barely notice.
Hmm. Okay, give me the one bag, and I'll fire a small test tile with the mix first.

questions.prompt: What is the conversation mainly about?
options: Repairing a sculpture that cracked during firing
Ordering a type of clay the studio doesn't stock
Reserving kiln time before a final deadline
Getting enough material for a large project
questions.explanation: The student needs much more clay than the studio can give her, and the attendant suggests another source.

questions.prompt: What is the student's attitude toward the reclaimed clay at first?
options: She thinks it costs too much for students.
She doubts that it is reliable enough.
She believes it is reserved for seniors.
She prefers it to the fresh clay.
questions.explanation: She worries that it is lumpy and could make her piece crack in the kiln.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and an attendant at the music practice room desk.

turns.text: Hi, I'm trying to book one of the rooms with a grand piano, but the system keeps saying I'm not eligible.
Are you a music major?
No, I'm in biology. But I'm auditioning for the music minor in two weeks, and the audition's on a grand piano. The uprights feel totally different.
Yeah, the grand rooms are reserved for majors during the day. But after nine at night, anything that's empty is open to everyone. You'd just sign in here.
After nine? I have an early lab most mornings, so that's tough.
Then talk to the piano faculty. If someone there sends us a short email saying you're auditioning, we can give you a temporary pass until the audition.
Oh, that's perfect. My audition's being organized by Professor Hale. I'll ask her today.

questions.prompt: Why does the student come to the desk?
options: He wants to change his major to music.
He needs to cancel a booking he made for late at night.
He cannot reserve a room with a grand piano.
He is looking for a new piano teacher.
questions.explanation: He says the booking system will not let him reserve a grand piano room.

questions.prompt: What will the student probably do next?
options: Practice on one of the upright pianos instead
Ask a faculty member to contact the desk
Sign in at the desk after nine tonight
Move his audition to a later date
questions.explanation: He says he will ask Professor Hale, who can email the desk so he gets a temporary pass.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and a staff member at the campus makerspace.

turns.text: Hi, I'd like to use the laser cutter. I want to make a wooden sign for my sister's birthday on Friday.
Sure. Have you done the safety training? The next session's Saturday morning, and we can't make exceptions. Those machines can start fires if they're set up wrong.
Saturday's too late. Could you maybe run it for me? I already have the design file.
Sorry, staff can't do personal projects. What's the design, though? Just lettering?
Yeah, her name and a little star.
Then try the vinyl cutter. You'd cut the letters out as a sticker and press them onto painted wood. That one only needs a fifteen-minute video, and you can watch it right over there.
Oh, that could actually look nice. Okay, where's the video?

questions.prompt: What is the student's problem?
options: He has not been certified to use a machine.
His design file will not open on the computer.
The makerspace has run out of wood for signs.
He missed a safety session he signed up for.
questions.explanation: He wants to use the laser cutter, but he has not completed the required safety training.

questions.prompt: What will the student probably do next?
options: Learn to use a different machine
Sign up for the laser training on Saturday
Ask another member to cut his design for him
Paint his sister's name onto the wood by hand
questions.explanation: He likes the idea of using the vinyl cutter and asks where to find its fifteen-minute training video.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and the editor of the student newspaper.

turns.text: Hi, I'm Grace. I emailed you last week about an opinion piece on the library closing at ten. Did you get a chance to read it?
I did. It's well written. The thing is, we ran almost the same argument in March, and it got a lot of responses.
Oh. So it's a no.

Not necessarily. Another opinion piece won't add much. But nobody's actually found out how many people are in the library at nine thirty. If you could get those numbers, maybe from the front desk's entry counts, that's a news story.
So you'd want facts instead of my argument.
Facts that make the argument for you, really. Readers trust numbers more than they trust columnists.
Okay. I'll ask the library for their counts this week.

questions.prompt: What is the conversation mainly about?
options: The editor's response to a piece the student wrote
A survey of students who use the library late at night
A job opening for a reporter at the newspaper
Readers' reactions to an article from March
questions.explanation: The student asks about her opinion piece, and the editor explains how she could change it.

questions.prompt: Why does the editor mention the article from March?
options: To explain why he hesitates to publish her column
To show that readers disagreed with her view
To suggest that she contact its original author
To prove that the library changed its hours
questions.explanation: He points out that the paper already ran almost the same argument, so another one would add little.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and the director of his residence hall.

turns.text: Hi, Ms. Nakamura. I wanted to ask about the bike rule. Is there any way I could get permission to keep my bike in my room?
Ah. Would this be the blue road bike that's been leaning against the wall outside room two-oh-eight?
Uh, yeah. Sorry. It's just, the racks outside are uncovered, and it's been raining for a week. The chain's already rusting.
I understand. But hallways need to stay clear for fire safety, and rooms aren't really an option either. Have you seen the storage room in the basement?
I heard it's always full.
It was, in September. But a lot of people took their bikes home over break and didn't bring them back. I can activate your key card for it today.
Oh, that'd be great. I'll move it down tonight.

questions.prompt: Why does the student go to see the director?
options: To report a bike that is blocking a hallway
To complain about rust on the outdoor racks
To request an exception to a building rule
To ask for a key to the basement laundry
questions.explanation: He asks whether he could get permission to keep his bike in his room, which the rules do not allow.

questions.prompt: What does the director imply when she mentions room two-oh-eight?
options: She already knows the student has broken the rule.
She wants the student to switch to a room on another floor.
She thinks the bike belongs to someone else.
She has received complaints about rain damage.
questions.explanation: She identifies his bike in the hallway outside his room, and he immediately apologizes.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and an officer at the campus police lost ID desk.

turns.text: Hi, I lost my student ID sometime yesterday. I already reported it online, but I can't get into my dorm or the dining hall without it.
Let's check the box first. People turn in a lot of cards here. What's your last name?
Moreno. Sofia Moreno.
Moreno. Here we go. Someone found it outside the science building this morning.
Oh, thank goodness! So I can just use it again?

Not quite. Since you reported it lost online, the system shut it off so nobody else could use it. You'll need to go to the ID card office to turn it back on. It's free, since you're not getting a new card.
Where's that office again?
Ground floor of the student center. They're open until four.

questions.prompt: What is the conversation mainly about?
options: Paying for a replacement student ID
Recovering a student ID that was turned in
Reporting a theft near the science building
Getting temporary access to a dining hall
questions.explanation: The officer finds the student's lost ID, which someone turned in that morning.

questions.prompt: Why must the student visit another office?
options: Her card was turned off after she reported it lost.
The card office keeps all of the cards that people find.
She needs to pay a fee for a new card.
The photo on her card is out of date.
questions.explanation: The officer explains that the system deactivated her card when she reported it lost online.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and a scheduler at the tutoring center.

turns.text: Hi, I'd like to set up weekly appointments with Mia, the organic chemistry tutor. A friend said she's really good.
She is, and that's the problem. Her schedule's full through the end of the semester.
Oh. Is there anyone else for organic chem?
Two other tutors, but they're mostly booked too. Have you thought about a group session? Mia actually runs one on Tuesday evenings. Up to six students, same material.
A group, hmm. I was hoping for one-on-one. I've got a lot of questions.
Understandable. I can put you on her waitlist as well. Students cancel more often than you'd think, especially after midterms.
Okay, let's do both. Sign me up for Tuesday, and put me on the list.

questions.prompt: Why does the student contact the tutoring center?
options: To apply for a job as a chemistry tutor
To cancel an appointment after midterms
To arrange regular sessions with a certain tutor
To complain about a group session he attended
questions.explanation: He asks to set up weekly appointments with Mia, the organic chemistry tutor.

questions.prompt: What does the student decide to do?
options: Find a different tutor for organic chemistry right away
Wait until after midterms to sign up
Join a group session and wait for an opening
Share his friend's time with the tutor
questions.explanation: He asks to be signed up for the Tuesday group and placed on Mia's waitlist.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and a clerk at the outdoor equipment rental center.

turns.text: Hi, I want to rent a four-person tent for this weekend. A few friends and I are going camping at the lake.
Let me check. Hmm, all our four-person tents are reserved through Sunday. It's a popular weekend because of the holiday.
Oh no. We already booked the campsite.
Well, I do have two-person tents left. You could take two of those. They're lighter to carry, actually.
Is that more expensive?

Two small ones cost the same as one big one, twenty-four dollars a night. The only difference is the deposit. It's twenty dollars for each tent, and you get it back when you return them clean and dry.
That's fine. I'll take two. Can I pick them up Friday morning?
Sure, any time after eight.

questions.prompt: What is the student's problem?
options: The size of tent she wanted is unavailable.
Her campsite reservation was cancelled.
She cannot afford the rental deposit.
The tent she rented last time was returned damaged.
questions.explanation: All of the four-person tents are reserved for the weekend.

questions.prompt: What does the man say about the deposit?
options: It is waived for holiday weekends.
It costs twenty-four dollars a night.
It is charged for each tent rented.
It is kept if a tent is returned late.
questions.explanation: He explains that the deposit is twenty dollars for each tent.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and the manager of the campus farm.

turns.text: Hi, I'm with the cooking club. We're holding a fundraising dinner next month, and we'd love to use vegetables from the farm. Could we buy some from you?
I wish I could say yes. But everything we grow is already promised to dining services. That's how the farm pays for itself.
Even a few boxes? We'd pay whatever they pay.

It's in the contract, unfortunately. Now, here's a thought. Saturday mornings are harvest days. Volunteers who stay the full shift each take home a share of whatever's left after the dining hall order.
How much is a share?
Depends on the week. In October, honestly, more squash than anyone knows what to do with.
Well, there are twelve of us in the club. If most of us come for a couple of Saturdays...
Then I'd say your menu's going to have a lot of squash in it.

questions.prompt: Why does the student visit the farm manager?
options: To sign up for a job with dining services
To ask the farm to cater a club dinner
To obtain produce for a club event
To complain about the dining hall's menu
questions.explanation: He asks whether the cooking club can buy the farm's vegetables for its fundraising dinner.

questions.prompt: What does the manager imply at the end of the conversation?
options: The club should hold its dinner at a later date.
Squash is the only crop dining services rejects.
The club could get lots of food by volunteering.
Twelve volunteers would be too many for one shift.
questions.explanation: Her joke about a menu full of squash suggests that volunteering would give the club a large share of vegetables.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and a clerk at the campus event ticket office.

turns.text: Hi, I bought two tickets online for the comedy show, but I just noticed they're for Thursday. I meant to get Saturday. I have a lab Thursday night.
Okay, we can exchange them. There's a two-dollar fee per ticket for exchanges, though.
That's fine. Are there still seats on Saturday?
Let me look. The main floor's sold out, but there are a few in the balcony. They're actually a little cheaper, so the difference would cover the fee.
Oh, nice. Can we sit together up there?
Yes, I have two together in the front row of the balcony. Honestly, those are some of the best seats for this kind of show. You can see the whole stage.
Great, let's do that.
Okay. I'll just need the card you paid with.

questions.prompt: What does the student want to do?
options: Get a refund for a cancelled show
Move from the balcony to seats on the main floor
Buy extra tickets for her lab partners
Switch her tickets to a different night
questions.explanation: She bought tickets for Thursday by mistake and wants Saturday instead.

questions.prompt: Why will the exchange cost the student nothing extra?
options: Exchanges are always free for students.
The clerk decides to waive the fee for her.
The new seats are cheaper than the old ones.
Her lab conflict counts as a valid excuse.
questions.explanation: The clerk says the balcony seats are cheaper, so the price difference covers the exchange fee.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and a coordinator at the scholarship office.

turns.text: Hi, Ms. Vasquez. My application for the Whitfield Scholarship is due Friday, but one of my recommendation letters still isn't uploaded.
Let's take a look. Yes, I see. Doctor Patel's letter is missing. Have you reminded her?
Twice. She's doing fieldwork in the mountains this month, and I don't think she has much internet. She said she'd send it, though.
Well, the good news is the committee accepts letters up to a week after the deadline. So submit everything else on time.
Okay, that helps.
Still, if she can't get a signal for another week... Is there anyone else who knows your work well?
My lab supervisor, maybe. I hadn't really thought about him.
It might be worth asking him. We'd use whichever letter arrives first.

questions.prompt: What is the student concerned about?
options: His professor refused to recommend him.
A required letter may not arrive in time.
The application deadline was moved earlier.
His supervisor does not know his work well.
questions.explanation: He says one recommendation letter is still missing and the writer has little internet access.

questions.prompt: What will the student probably do?
options: Wait until Doctor Patel returns from fieldwork
Submit his application a week after Friday
Withdraw his application until next year
Request a second letter as a backup
questions.explanation: The coordinator suggests asking his lab supervisor, and the office will use whichever letter arrives first.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and a receptionist at the counseling center.

turns.text: Hi, I saw a flyer for a workshop on managing study time during exams. Is this where I sign up?
It is. Let me check. Oh, I'm sorry. Thursday's session filled up yesterday.
Oh. Exams start in three weeks, so I was hoping to get in soon.

There's a second session two weeks from Thursday, which is still before exams. And in the meantime, there's a short online version on our website. It covers the basics, like breaking big tasks into smaller ones.
Is the second session the same as the first one?
Yes, same leader, same material. A lot of students do the online part first and then come with questions.
Okay, put me down for the second one, then.
Sure. Can I get your name and student email?

questions.prompt: Why does the student go to the counseling center?
options: To speak with the leader of a workshop
To ask for a printed copy of her exam schedule
To register for a workshop on study time
To post a flyer for a student event
questions.explanation: She asks where to sign up for the workshop she saw on a flyer.

questions.prompt: What does the man say about the online version?
options: Many students complete it before attending.
It replaces the in-person session for most students.
It is only available after exams.
It is led by a different person.
questions.explanation: He says many students do the online part first and then bring their questions to the session.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and an attendant at the campus laundry service.

turns.text: Hi, I picked up my wash-and-fold order yesterday, but when I opened the bag at home, these weren't my clothes.
Oh no, I'm so sorry. Can I see the tag on the bag?
Here. It says Larson. My name's Arjun Mehta.
Okay, so the bags got switched. Do you have your claim slip?
Yeah, here it is. Number four-oh-two.
Let me check the back. Here we go, four-oh-two, still on the shelf. Someone must've grabbed the wrong bag earlier, and we gave you what was left.
So the other person hasn't come in?
Not yet. I'll keep this bag for them. And since this was our mistake, your next order is free. I'll write it on your slip.

questions.prompt: What is the student's problem?
options: Some of his clothes were damaged in the wash.
He was given another customer's laundry.
He lost the claim slip for his order.
His order was not ready when promised.
questions.explanation: When he opened the bag at home, the clothes inside belonged to someone else.

questions.prompt: What does the woman offer the student?
options: A refund for yesterday's order
His next order at no charge
Delivery of the bag to his home
A new number for his claim slip
questions.explanation: She says his next order is free because the switch was the laundry's mistake.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and a worker at the student union information desk.

turns.text: Hi, I'd like to put up some flyers for my chess club's tournament. Can I just pin them on the boards by the entrance?
Almost. Everything on those boards needs an approval stamp from this desk first. Otherwise, the cleaning staff take it down at night.
Oh, okay. Can you stamp them now? I have twenty.
Sure. But we only allow five per event, so that one group doesn't cover the whole board.
Five? Hmm. Then what do I do with the rest?
You could try the residence halls, though they have their own rules. Or, honestly, the digital screens might reach more people. You just submit an image online, and it runs for a week.
Oh, I didn't know about those. I'll do both, then. Five here, and the screens.

questions.prompt: Why does the student go to the information desk?
options: To sign up for a chess tournament
To find out how to advertise a club event
To report flyers that the cleaning staff took down
To reserve a room for his club
questions.explanation: He asks about putting up flyers for his chess club's tournament.

questions.prompt: Why do flyers need a stamp from the desk?
options: Unstamped flyers are removed at night.
Stamped flyers also appear on the screens.
The residence halls require the same stamp.
Stamps show which club paid a fee.
questions.explanation: The worker says the cleaning staff take down anything without an approval stamp.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and an officer at the alumni office.

turns.text: Hi. I'm hoping to talk to some graduates who work in marine conservation. Could you give me a list of names and emails?
I can't share personal contact details, I'm afraid. Alumni give us that information with the understanding that it stays with us.
Oh. I didn't think about that. I just wanted to ask a few people how they got started.

Which is exactly what a lot of them like to talk about. Here's what we can do. If you write a short message, a paragraph about who you are and what you'd like to know, I'll forward it to alumni in that field. Whoever's interested replies to you directly.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and the coordinator of the language lab.

turns.text: Hi, I signed up for the conversation partner program last month, hoping to practice Japanese. I haven't heard anything back.
Let me see. Yes, you're on the list. The problem is, we only have four Japanese exchange students this year, and they're all paired already.
Oh. So that's it until next year?
Not necessarily. There's a Japanese conversation table every Thursday at lunch. Several exchange students come, and so do a few teachers.
I've heard about that. I'm just... I'm only in second-year Japanese. Everyone there probably talks really fast.
Some do. But plenty of people at your level go, and the first few times, most of them mainly listen. Nobody minds.
Well, I guess listening's better than nothing. Maybe I'll go this Thursday and see what it's like.

questions.prompt: What is the conversation mainly about?
options: Choosing a Japanese course for next year
Becoming a conversation partner for an exchange student
Organizing a lunch for language teachers
Finding the student a way to practice speaking
questions.explanation: He has not been matched with a partner, and the coordinator suggests another way to practice Japanese.

questions.prompt: How does the student feel about the conversation table?
options: Excited, because his partner will be there
Doubtful that any teachers will attend
Nervous, but willing to give it a try
Confident that his Japanese is good enough
questions.explanation: He worries that everyone speaks fast but decides to go once and see what it is like.

intro: Listen to a conversation between a student and a librarian at the public library.

turns.text: Hi, I got an email saying our Tuesday room reservation was cancelled for the rest of the month. I run a study group, and we meet in Room B.
Let me check. Ah, yes. The system cancels standing reservations after two no-shows. It looks like nobody checked in on the third or the tenth.
Oh. We met online those two weeks because of the snow. I guess I never cancelled the room.
That happens. Unfortunately, once it's released, other groups can book it, and someone's already taken Room B for the next two Tuesdays.
Is there anything else available?
Room D is free. It's smaller and doesn't have a screen, but it fits six.
There are five of us, and we mostly use the whiteboard anyway. We'll take it. And I'll cancel properly next time.

questions.prompt: Why does the student go to the library desk?
options: To report that the snow closed the library
To join a study group that meets on Tuesdays
To complain that Room B has no screen
To ask about a booking that was taken away
questions.explanation: She received an email saying her group's Tuesday reservation was cancelled.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about Room D?
options: It is larger than Room B.
It has a screen the group can use.
It will meet the group's needs.
It was booked on the third and tenth.
questions.explanation: Room D fits six people and her group of five mostly uses the whiteboard, so she accepts it.
